SAVANT: A man of learning; one versed in literature or science; a person eminent for acquirements.
SHOTE: 1. (Zoöl.) A fish resembling the trout. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Garew. 2. Etym: [Perh. a different word.] A young hog; a shoat.
SOFTA: Any one attached to a Mohammedan mosque, esp. a student of the higher branches of theology in a mosque school. [Written also sophta.]
SCHWENKFELDER: A member of a religious sect founded by Kaspar von Schwenkfeld, a Silesian reformer who disagreed with Luther, especially on the deification of the body of Christ.

SNUFFER: 1. One who snuffs. 2. (Zoöl.) The common porpoise.
SPERLING: (a) A smelt; a sparling. [Prov. Eng.] (b) A young herring. [Local, U.S.]
SULU: A member of the most prominent tribe of the Moro tribes, occupying the Sulu Archipelago; also, their language.
SMOOTHING: fr. Smooth, v. Smoothing iron, an iron instrument with a polished face, for smoothing clothes; a sadiron; a flatiron. -- Smoothing plane, a short, finely set plane, for smoothing and finishing work.
SCRINE: A chest, bookcase, or other place, where writings or curiosities are deposited; a shrine. [Obs.] But laid them up in immortial scrine. Spenser. To cringe. [Prov. Eng. & Local, U.S.]
SALTANT: 1. Leaping; jumping; dancing. 2. (Her.) In a leaping position; springing forward; -- applied especially to the squirrel, weasel, and rat, also to the cat, greyhound, monkey, etc.
SAVIOR: 1. One who saves, preserves, or delivers from destruction or danger. 2. Specifically: The (or our, your, etc.) Savior, he who brings salvation to men; Jesus Christ, the Redeemer.
SOLA: See Solus. A leguminous plant (Æschynomene aspera) growing in moist places in Southern India and the East Indies. Its pithlike stem is used for making hats, swimming-jackets, etc. [Written also solah, shola.] Alone; -- chiefly used in stage directions, and the like.
STREAKY: Same as Streaked, 1. "The streaky west." Cowper.
SULPHINDIGOTIC: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a sulphonic acid obtained, as a blue solution, by dissolving indigo in sulphuric acid; -- formerly called also cerulic sulphuric acid, but properly called indigo-disulphonic acid.
SLIDOMETER: An instrument for indicating and recording shocks to railway cars occasioned by sudden stopping.
SINCERELY: In a sincere manner. Specifically: (a) Purely; without alloy. Milton. (b) Honestly; unfeignedly; without dissimulation; as, to speak one's mind sincerely; to love virtue sincerely.
SUM: 1. The aggregate of two or more numbers, magnitudes, quantities, or particulars; the amount or whole of any number of individuals or particulars added together; as, the sum of 5 and 7 is 12. SUPERCARPAL: Situated above, or in the upper part of, the carpus.
STEELHEAD: 1. (Zoöl.) A North Pacific salmon (Salmo Gairdneri) found from Northern California to Siberia; -- called also hardhead, and preesil. 2. (Zoöl.) The ruddy duck.
SNOOZE: A short sleep; a nap. [Colloq.] To doze; to drowse; to take a short nap; to slumber. [Colloq.]
SIGNETED: Stamped or marked with a signet.
SUPPORTRESS: A female supporter. [R.] You are my gracious patroness and supportress. Massinger.

STRAIT-JACKET: A dress of strong materials for restraining maniacs or those who are violently delirious. It has long sleeves, which are closed at the ends, confining the hands, and may be tied behind the back.
SISE: An assize. [Obs.] Six; the highest number on a die; the cast of six in throwing dice. In the new casting of a die, when ace is on the top, sise must needs be at the bottom. Fuller.
SEMINATE: To sow; to spread; to propagate. [R.] Waterhouse.
SPIRED: Having a spire; being in the form of a spire; as, a spired steeple. Mason.
SLIVE: To sneak. [Prov. Eng.] To cut; to split; to separate. [Obs.] Holland.
SUBDEACON: One belonging to an order in the Roman Catholic Church, next interior to the order of deacons; also, a member of a minor order in the Greek Church.
SUBMULTIPLE: A number or quality which is contained in another an exact number of times, or is an aliquot part of it; thus, 7 is the submultiple of 56, being contained in it eight times. Of or pertaining to a submultiple; being a submultiple; as, a submultiple number; submultiple ratio.
STILLIFORM: Having the form of a drop. Owen.
SANCTUARY: A sacred place; a consecrated spot; a holy and inviolable site. SICKLEMAN: One who uses a sickle; a reaper. You sunburned sicklemen, of August weary. Shak.

A goatsucker; -- so called from the peculiar noise it makes when darting through the air. 4. (Zoöl.) A spinneret. SANTAL: A colorless crystalline substance, isomeric with piperonal, but having weak acid properties. It is extracted from sandalwood.
SENESCENT: Growing old; decaying with the lapse of time. "The night was senescent." Poe. "With too senescent air." Lowell.
STORER: One who lays up or forms a store.
STIPULATION: 1. The act of stipulating; a contracting or bargaining; an agreement. 2. SCAUPER: A tool with a semicircular edge, -- used by engravers to clear away the spaces between the lines of an engraving. Fairholt.
SIGNIORSHIP: State or position of a signior.
SPENDER: One who spends; esp., one who spends lavishly; a prodigal; a spendthrift.
SHILOH: A word used by Jacob on his deathbed, and interpreted variously, as "the Messiah," or as the city "Shiloh," or as "Rest."
SETOSE: Thickly set with bristles or bristly hairs.

SOCOME: A custom of tenants to grind corn at the lord's mill. Cowell.
SELDOM: Rarely; not often; not frequently. Wisdom and youth are seldom joined in one. Hooker. Rare; infrequent. [Archaic.] "A suppressed and seldom anger." Jer. Taylor.
SEA APE: (a) The thrasher shark. (b) The sea otter.
STALWART: Brave; bold; strong; redoubted; daring; vehement; violent. "A stalwart tiller of the soil." Prof. Wilson. Fair man be was and wise, stalworth and bold. R. of Brunne. Note: Stalworth is now disused, or bur little used, stalwart having taken its place.
SPHENOID: 1. Wedge-shaped; as, a sphenoid crystal. 2. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the sphenoid bone. SHEET ANCHOR: 1. (Naut.) A large anchor stowed on shores outside the waist of a vessel; -- called also waist anchor. See the Note under Anchor. 2. Anything regarded as a sure support or dependence in danger; the best hope or refuge.
SIGHTLY: 1. Pleasing to the sight; comely. "Many brave, sightly horses." L'Estrange. 2. Open to sight; conspicuous; as, a house stands in a sightly place.
SALVABLE: Capable of being saved; admitting of salvation. Dr. H. More. -- Sal"va*ble*ness, n. -- Sal"va*bly, adv.
STAR-BOWLINES: The men in the starboard watch. [Obs.] R. H. Dana, Jr.
SPONDEE: A poetic foot of two long syllables, as in the Latin word leges.
SELF-UNED: One with itself; separate from others. [Obs.] Sylvester.
SQUEEGEE ROLLER: A small India-rubber roller with a handle, used esp. in printing and photography as a squeegee.
SNOTTER: To snivel; to cry or whine. [Prov. Eng.] Grose. A rope going over a yardarm, used to bend a tripping line to, in sending down topgallant and royal yards in vessels of war; also, the short line supporting the heel of the sprit in a small boat.
SEMICENTENNIAL: Of or pertaining to half of a century, or a period of fifty years; as, a semicentennial commemoration. A fiftieth anniversary.
SPANAEMIA: A condition of impoverishment of the blood; a morbid state in which the red corpuscles, or other important elements of the blood, are deficient.
SICILIAN: Of or pertaining to Sicily or its inhabitants. Sicilian vespers, the great massacre of the French in Sicily, in the year 1282, on the evening of Easter Monday, at the hour of vespers. A native or inhabitant of Sicily.
SULLIAGE: Foulness; filth. [Obs.] Though we wipe away with never so much care the dirt thrown at us, there will be left some sulliage behind. Gov. of Tongue.
SENSIST: One who, in philosophy, holds to sensism.
SEARCHER: One who, or that which, searhes or examines; a seeker; an inquirer; an examiner; a trier. SEDAN: A portable chair or covered vehicle for carrying a single person, -- usually borne on poles by two men. Called also sedan chair.
SORITICAL: Of or pertaining to a sorites; resembling a sorites.
SHOGGLE: To joggle. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Pegge.
SMELL: 1. SECTIONALITY: The state or quality of being sectional; sectionalism.
STAKTOMETER: A drop measurer; a glass tube tapering to a small orifice at the point, and having a bulb in the middle, used for finding the number of drops in equal quantities of different liquids. See Pipette. Sir D. Brewster.
SELF-WORSHIP: The idolizing of one's self; immoderate self-conceit.
SCULPTOR: 1. One who sculptures; one whose occupation is to carve statues, or works of sculpture. 2. Hence, an artist who designs works of sculpture, his first studies and his finished model being usually in a plastic material, from which model the marble is cut, or the bronze is cast.
SABOT: 1. A kind of wooden shoe worn by the peasantry in France, Belgium, Sweden, and some other European countries. 2. (Mil.) A thick, circular disk of wood, to which the cartridge bag and projectile are attached, in fixed ammunition for cannon; also, a piece of soft metal attached to a projectile to take the groove of the rifling.
SHOOK: imp. & obs. or poet. p. p. of Shake. (a) A set of staves and headings sufficient in number for one hogshead, cask, barrel, or the like, trimmed, and bound together in compact form. SHEDDER: 1. One who, or that which, sheds; as, a shedder of blood; a shedder of tears. 2. (Zoöl.) A crab in the act of casting its shell, or immediately afterwards while still soft; -- applied especially to the edible crabs, which are most prized while in this state.
SAUTE: An assault. [Obs.] p. p. of Sauter. C. Owen.
SALIVATION: The act or process of salivating; an excessive secretion of saliva, often accompained with soreness of the mouth and gums; ptyalism. Note: It may be induced by direct chemical or mechanical stimulation, as in mastication of some tasteless substance like rubber, or indirectly by some agent which affects the whole system, as mercury compounds.
SEPTUAGESIMA: The third Sunday before Lent; -- so called because it is about seventy days before Easter.

SATYRIASIS: Immoderate venereal appetite in the male. Quain.
SYNCLINAL: 1. Inclined downward from opposite directions, so as to meet in a common point or line. 2. (Geol.) Formed by strata dipping toward a common line or plane; as, a synclinal trough or valley; a synclinal fold; -- opposed to anticlinal. SQUEEZER: 1. One who, or that which, squeezes; as, a lemon squeezer. 2. (Forging) (a) A machine like a large pair of pliers, for shingling, or squeezing, the balls of metal when puddled; -- used only in the plural. (b) A machine of several forms for the same purpose; -- used in the singular.
SEA MUD: A rich slimy deposit in salt marshes and along the seashore, sometimes used as a manure; -- called also sea ooze.
SALIRETIN: A yellow amorphous resinoid substance obtained by the action of dilute acids on saligenin.
SPLEENLESS: Having no spleen; hence, kind; gentle; mild. [Obs.] Chapman.
SCALING: 1. Adapted for removing scales, as from a fish; as, a scaling knife; adapted for removing scale, as from the interior of a steam boiler; as, a scaling hammer, bar, etc. 2. Serving as an aid in clambering; as, a scaling ladder, used in assaulting a fortified place.
SYNODIST: An adherent to a synod. These synodists thought fit in Latin as yet to veil their decrees from vulgar eyes. Fuller.
SEPARATICAL: Of or pertaining to separatism in religion; schismatical. [R.] Dr. T. Dwight.
SICKER: To percolate, trickle, or ooze, as water through a crack. [Also written sigger, zigger, and zifhyr.] [Prov. Eng.] Sure; certain; trusty. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Burns. SURFY: Consisting of, abounding in, or resembling, surf; as, a surfy shore. Scarce had they cleared the surfy waves That foam around those frightful caves. Moore.
SWEENY: An atrophy of the muscles of the shoulder in horses; also, atrophy of any muscle in horses. [Written also swinney.]
STEREOMETRY: The art of measuring and computing the cubical contents of bodies and figures; -- distinguished from planimetry.
STYLOHYOID: Of or pertaining to the styloid process and the hyoid bone.
STRISORES: A division of passerine birds including the humming birds, swifts, and goatsuckers. It is now generally considered an artificial group.
SUDRA: The lowest of the four great castes among the Hindoos. See Caste. [Written also Soorah, Soodra, and Sooder.]

STRAW-CUTTER: An instrument to cut straw for fodder.
SUBSESQUI-: A prefix (also used adjectively) denoting the combination of constituents (especially electro-negative and electro-positive bodies) in the proportion of two to three; as, a subsesqui acetate, i. e., a salt having two equivalents of acetic acid to three of the base.
SUBCOMPRESSED: Not fully compressed; partially or somewhat compressed.
STETHOSCOPY: The art or process of examination by the stethoscope.
STERNMOST: Farthest in the rear; farthest astern; as, the sternmost ship in a convoy.
SEMAPHORIC: Of or pertaining to a semaphore, or semaphores; telegraphic.
SEQUESTERED: Retired; secluded. "Sequestered scenes." Cowper. Along the cool, sequestered vale of life. Gray.

SHETH: The part of a plow which projects downward beneath the beam, for holding the share and other working parts; -- also called standard, or post.
STEENING: A lining made of brick, stone, or other hard material, as for a well. [Written also steaning.]
STRANGLER: One who, or that which, strangles. "The very strangler of their amity." Shak.
SODAIC: Pertaining to, or containing, soda. "Sodaic powder." Ure.

SANTEES: One of the seven confederated tribes of Indians belonging to the Sioux, or Dakotas.
SUBDEAN: An under dean; the deputy or substitute of a dean. Ayliffe.
STATIC: 1. Resting; acting by mere weight without motion; as, statical pressure; static objects. 2. Pertaining to bodies at rest or in equilibrium. Statical electricity. See Note under Electricity, 1. -- Statical moment. See under Moment.
SCHOLIAST: A maker of scholia; a commentator or annotator. No . . . quotations from Talmudists and scholiasts . . . ever marred the effect of his grave temperate discourses. Macaulay.
SYNDESMOSIS: An articulation formed by means of ligaments.
SCRUPULOUS: 1. Full ofscrupules; inclined to scruple; nicely doubtful; hesitating to determine or to act, from a fear of offending or of doing wrong. STYLIFORM: Having the form of, or resembling, a style, pin, or pen; styloid.
SCOURER: 1. One who, or that which, scours. 2. A rover or footpad; a prowling robber. In those days of highwaymen and scourers. Macaulay.
SYLLEPSIS: 1. (Rhet.) A figure of speech by which a word is used in a literal and metaphorical sense at the same time. 2. (Gram.) The agreement of a verb or adjective with one, rather than another, of two nouns, with either of which it might agree in gender, number, etc.; as, rex et regina beati.
SYMPLOCE: The repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning and another at the end of successive clauses; as, Justice came down from heaven to view the earth; Justice returned to heaven, and left the earth.
SYSTALTIC: Capable of, or taking place by, alternate contraction and dilatation; as, the systaltic action of the heart.
STRAP: 1. A long, narrow, pliable strip of leather, cloth, or the like; specifically, a strip of thick leather used in flogging. SCISSOR: To cut with scissors or shears; to prepare with the aid of scissors. Massinger.
STAMINAL: Of or pertaining to stamens or stamina; consisting in stamens.
STATISTIC: Of or pertaining to statistics; as, statistical knowledge, statistical tabulation.
SHEENY: Bright; shining; radiant; sheen. "A sheeny summer morn." Tennyson.
STEEL: 1. (Metal) A variety of iron intermediate in composition and properties between wrought iron and cast iron (containing between one half of one per cent and one and a half per cent of carbon), and consisting of an alloy of iron with an iron carbide. SEDERUNT: A sitting, as of a court or other body. 'T is pity we have not Burn's own account of that long sederunt. Prof. Wilson. Acts of sederunt (Scots Law), ordinances of the Court of Session for the ordering of processes and expediting of justice. Bell.
STARCHY: Consisting of starch; resembling starch; stiff; precise.
STRIPPET: A small stream. [Obs.] "A little brook or strippet." Holinshed.
SAMARA: A dry, indehiscent, usually one-seeded, winged fruit, as that of the ash, maple, and elm; a key or key fruit.
SOCIOLOGY: That branch of philosophy which treats of the constitution, phenomena, and development of human society; social science. H. Spencer.
SUPPURATE: To generate pus; as, a boil or abscess suppurates. To cause to generate pus; as, to suppurate a sore. Arbuthnot.
SNATTOCK: A chip; a alice. [Prov. Eng.] Gayton.
SOONER: In the western United States, one who settles on government land before it is legally open to settlement in order to gain the prior claim that the law gives to the first settler when the land is opened to settlement; hence, any one who does a thing prematurely or anticipates another in acting in order to gain an unfair advantage.
STIGMATICAL: 1. Marked with a stigma, or with something reproachful to character. 2. Impressing with infamy or reproach. [R.] 3. (Bot., Anat., etc) Of or pertaining to a stigma or stigmata. SCRAWLER: One who scrawls; a hasty, awkward writer.
SELF-PRESERVATION: The preservation of one's self from destruction or injury.
STIPULA: 1. (Bot.) A stipule. 2. (Zoöl.) A newly sprouted feather.
SOVEREIGN: 1. Supreme or highest in power; superior to all others; chief; as, our sovereign prince. 2. SADH: A member of a monotheistic sect of Hindoos. Sadhs resemble the Quakers in many respects. Balfour (cyc. of India).
SUBVAGINAL: Situated under or inside a sheath or vaginal membrane; as, the subvaginal, or subdural, spaces about the optic nerve.

SOUPE-MAIGRE: Soup made chiefly from vegetables or fish with a little butter and a few condiments.
SUBSEXTUPLE: Having the ratio of one to six; as, a subsextuple proportion. Bp. Wilkins.
SUPRA-ETHMOID: Above, or on the dorsal side of, the ethmoid bone or cartilage.
SYCAMORE: (a) A large tree (Ficus Sycomorus) allied to the common fig. It is found in Egypt and Syria, and is the sycamore, or sycamine, of Scripture. (b) The American plane tree, or buttonwood. (c) A large European species of maple (Acer Pseudo-Platanus). [Written sometimes sycomore.]
SERINE: A white crystalline nitrogenous substance obtained by the action of dilute sulphuric acid on silk gelatin.
SWORDPLAYER: A fencer; a gladiator; one who exhibits his skill in the use of the sword.
SUSPIRED: Ardently desired or longed for; earnestly coveted. [Obs.] Sir H. Wotton.
SAINT-SIMONIANISM: The principles, doctrines, or practice of the Saint-Simonians; -- called also Saint-Simonism.
SIGMODONT: Any one of a tribe (Sigmodontes) of rodents which includes all the indigenous rats and mice of America. So called from the form of the ridges of enamel on the crowns of the worn molars. Also used adjectively.
SHAKESPEAREAN: Of, pertaining to, or in the style of, Shakespeare or his works. [Written also Shakespearian, Shakspearean, Shakspearian, Shaksperean, Shaksperian.etc.]
SPA: A spring or mineral water; -- so called from a place of this name in Belgium.
SYDEROLITE: A kind of Bohemian earthenware resembling the Wedgwood ware.
SALTER: One who makes, sells, or applies salt; one who salts meat or fish.

SIGHTLINESS: The state of being sightly; comeliness; conspicuousness.

SLOPSELLER: One who sells slops, or ready-made clothes. See 4th Slop, 3.

SQUAMELLATE: Furnished or covered with little scales; squamulose.
SELF-INTEREST: Private interest; the interest or advantage of one's self.

SAHEB: A respectful title or appelation given to Europeans of rank. [India]

SPOROCARP: (a) A closed body or conceptacle containing one or more masses of spores or sporangia. (b) A sporangium.
SISTER-IN-LAW: The sister of one's husband or wife; also, the wife of one's brother; sometimes, the wife of one's husband's or wife's brother.

SALESMAN: One who sells anything; one whose occupation is to sell goods or merchandise.

SHELDAPLE: A chaffinch. [Written also sheldapple, and shellapple.]
SINICAL: Of or pertaining to a sine; employing, or founded upon, sines; as, a sinical quadrant.

SARCOCOL: A gum resin obtained from certain shrubs of Africa (Penæa), -- formerly thought to cause healing of wounds and ulcers.
SHRAPE: A place baited with chaff to entice birds. [Written also scrap.] [Obs.] Bp. Bedell.
SELF-ASSERTING: asserting one's self, or one's own rights or claims; hence, putting one's self forward in a confident or assuming manner.
SYSTEMATIST: 1. One who forms a system, or reduces to system. 2. One who adheres to a system.

SESQUIALTERA: A stop on the organ, containing several ranks of pipes which reënforce some of the high harmonics of the ground tone, and make the sound more brilliant.

SEISMOGRAPH: An apparatus for registering the shocks and undulatory motions of earthquakes.
SELF-MOTION: Motion given by inherent power, without external impulse; spontaneus or voluntary motion. Matter is not induced with self-motion. Cheyne.
SUFFRAGE: 1. A vote given in deciding a controverted question, or in the choice of a man for an office or trust; the formal expression of an opinion; assent; vote. SAENGERFEST: A festival of singers; a German singing festival.
SHORTHORN: One of a breed of large, heavy domestic cattle having short horns. The breed was developed in England.
SMUTCH: A stain; a dirty spot. B. Jonson. To blacken with smoke, soot, or coal. [Written also smooch.] B. Jonson.
SPECIFICNESS: The quality or state of being specific.

SALVOR: One who assists in saving a ship or goods at sea, without being under special obligation to do so. Wheaton.
SANATIVE: Having the power to cure or heal; healing; tending to heal; sanatory. -- San"a*tive*ness, n.

SELF-RELIANCE: Reliance on one's own powers or judgment; self-trust.
SWANG: imp. of Swing. A swamp. [Prov. Eng.]

SELF-WILL: One's own will, esp. when opposed to that of others; obstinacy.

SPECTROGRAM: A photograph, map, or diagram of a spectrum.
SHAMBLING: Characterized by an awkward, irregular pace; as, a shambling trot; shambling legs. An awkward, irregular gait.
SOMATOLOGY: 1. The dictrine or the science of the general properties of material substances; somatics. 2. A treatise on the human body; anatomy. Dunglison.

SEISMOLOGICAL: Of or pertaining to seismology. -- Seis`mo*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

SELF-DISTRUST: Want of confidence in one' self; diffidence.
SELF-SACRIFICE: The act of sacrificing one's self, or one's interest, for others; self-devotion.
SHEALING: The outer husk, pod, or shell, as of oats, pease, etc.; sheal; shell. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Same as Sheeling. [Scot.]
SCRUTABLE: Discoverable by scrutiny, inquiry, or critical examination. [R.] r. H. More.
SPINE-FINNED: Having fine supported by spinous fin rays; -- said of certain fishes.
SERRULATE: Finely serrate; having very minute teeth.
STRAPPLE: To hold or bind with, or as with, a strap; to entangle. [Obs.] Chapman.

SINUATE: Having the margin alternately curved inward and outward; having rounded lobes separated by rounded sinuses; sinuous; wavy. To bend or curve in and out; to wind; to turn; to be sinusous. Woodward.

SELF-IMPOSED: Voluntarily taken on one's self; as, self-imposed tasks.
STILAR: Of or pertaining to the style of a dial. [Written also stylar.]
SUMMITY: 1. The height or top of anything. [Obs.] Swift. 2. The utmost degree; perfection. [Obs.] Hallywell.
SUING: The process of soaking through anything. [Obs.] Bacon.
SENSITIZER: An agent that sensitizes. The sensitizer should be poured on the middle of the sheet. Wilis & Clements (The Platinotype).

SLAVONIAN: 1. Of or pertaining to Slavonia, or its inhabitants. 2. Of or pertaining to the Slavs, or their language. A native or inhabitant of Slavonia; ethnologically, a Slav.

Comparative obscurity owing to interception or interruption of the rays of light; partial darkness caused by the intervention of something between the space contemplated and the source of light. SOBERLY: In a sober manner; temperately; cooly; calmly; gravely; seriously. Grave; serious; solemn; sad. [Obs.] [He] looked hollow and thereto soberly. Chaucer.
SWAIN: 1. A servant. [Obs.] Him behoves serve himself that has no swain. Chaucer. 2. A young man dwelling in the country; a rustic; esp., a cuntry gallant or lover; -- chiefly in poetry. SCURFY: Having or producing scurf; covered with scurf; resembling scurf.
SYRTIS: A quicksand. Quenched in a boggy syrtis, neither sea Nor good dry land. Milton.

SMIFT: A match for firing a charge of powder, as in blasting; a fuse.
SKETCHY: Containing only an outline or rough form; being in the manner of a sketch; incomplete. The execution is sketchy throughout; the head, in particular, is left in the rough. J. S. Harford.
SPLIT DYNAMOMETER: An electric dynamometer having two coils so arranged that one carries the primary current, and the other the secondary current, of a transformer.
SNIFFLE: To snuffle, as one does with a catarrh. [Prov. Eng.]
SCULP: To sculpture; to carve; to engrave. [Obs. or Humorous.] Sandys.
SKIN-DEEP: Not deeper than the skin; hence, superficial. Lowell.
SYCOCERIC: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained by the oxidation of sycoceryl alcohol.
SLIPPINESS: Slipperiness. [R.] "The slippiness of the way." Sir W. Scott.
SPORIDIUM: (a) A secondary spore, or a filament produced from a spore, in certain kinds of minute fungi. (b) A spore.
SOLIDUNGULA: A tribe of ungulates which includes the horse, ass, and related species, constituting the family Equidæ.
SKILTS: A kind of large, coarse, short trousers formerly worn. [Local, U. S.] Bartlett.

Of or pertaining to society; relating to men living in society, or to the public as an aggregate body; as, social interest or concerns; social pleasure; social benefits; social happiness; social duties. STAYMAKER: One whose occupation is to make stays.
SAUSEFLEM: Having a red, pimpled face. [Obs.] [Written also sawceflem.] Chaucer.
STEATITE: A massive variety of talc, of a grayish green or brown color. It forms extensive beds, and is quarried for fireplaces and for coarse utensils. Called also potstone, lard stone, and soapstone.
SCHETICAL: Of or pertaining to the habit of the body; constitutional. [Obs.] Cudworth.
STRELITZ: A soldier of the ancient Muscovite guard or Russian standing army; also, the guard itself.
SCALINESS: The state of being scaly; roughness.
STRATEGUS: The leader or commander of an army; a general.
SALINENESS: The quality or state of being salt; saltness.
SURCHARGEMENT: The act of surcharging; also, surcharge, surplus. [Obs.] Daniel.

SHARER: One who shares; a participator; a partaker; also, a divider; a distributer.
SPOILSMAN: One who serves a cause or a party for a share of the spoils; in United States politics, one who makes or recognizes a demand for public office on the ground of partisan service; also, one who sanctions such a policy in appointments to the public service.
SKINK: Any one of numerous species of regularly scaled harmless lizards of the family Scincidæ, common in the warmer parts of all the continents. SLIK: Such. [Obs. or Scot.] Note: Used by Chaucer as of the Northern dialect.
SHRILL-GORGED: Having a throat which produces a shrill note. [R.] Shak.
SUCCUSSION: The act of shaking; a shake; esp. (Med.), a shaking of the body to ascertain if there be a liquid in the thorax.

SAMOAN: Of or pertaining to the Samoan Islands (formerly called Navigators' Islands) in the South Pacific Ocean, or their inhabitants. -- n. An inhabitant of the Samoan Islands.
SEJUNCTION: The act of disjoining, or the state of being disjoined. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.

SUCHWISE: In a such a manner; so.
SAINTSHIP: The character or qualities of a saint.

SUPERNATURALITY: The quality or state of being supernatural.

SALISBURIA: The ginkgo tree (Ginkgo biloba, or Salisburia adiantifolia).

SUBTENSE: A line subtending, or stretching across; a chord; as, the subtense of an arc.

SIGLA: The signs, abbreviations, letters, or characters standing for words, shorthand, etc., in ancient manuscripts, or on coins, medals, etc. W. Savage.

SALSUGINOUS: Growing in brackish places or in salt marches.

SELF-LIFE: Life for one's self; living solely or chiefly for one's own pleasure or good.

SYNANGIUM: The divided part beyond the pylangium in the aortic trunk of the amphibian heart. -- Syn*an"gi*al, a.

STREAMING: Sending forth streams. 1. The act or operation of that which streams; the act of that which sends forth, or which runs in, streams. 2. (Mining) The reduction of stream tin; also, the search for stream tin.

STOMACHAL: 1. Of or pertaining to the stomach; gastric. 2. Helping the stomach; stomachic; cordial. A stomachic. Dunglison.
SALESWOMAN: A woman whose occupation is to sell goods or merchandise.
STEREOMONOSCOPE: An instrument with two lenses, by which an image of a single picture projected upon a screen of ground glass is made to present an appearance of relief, and may be viewed by several persons at once.
SPALE: 1. A lath; a shaving or chip, as of wood or stone. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] 2. (Shipbuilding) A strengthening cross timber.
SPOILSMONGER: One who promises or distributes public offices and their emoluments as the price of services to a party or its leaders.

SWARE: imp. of Swear. [Obs. or Poetic] Cophetua sware a royal oath. Tennyson.
SUTTEEISM: The practice of self-immolation of widows in Hindostan.
STUD-HORSE: A stallion, esp. one kept for breeding.
SAILING: 1. The act of one who, or that which, sails; the motion of a vessel on water, impelled by wind or steam; the act of starting on a voyage. 2. (Naut.) SERPENTARIUS: A constellation on the equator, lying between Scorpio and Hercules; -- called also Ophiuchus.
SHEAFY: Pertaining to, or consisting of, a sheaf or sheaves; resembling a sheaf.

SCAMBLINGLY: In a scambling manner; with turbulence and noise; with bold intrusiveness.

SPIRITUALIZATION: The act of spiritualizing, or the state of being spiritualized.
SELF-ELECTIVE: Having the right of electing one's self, or, as a body, of electing its own members.

SWASHING: 1. Swaggering; hectoring. "A swashing and martial outside." Shak. 2. Resounding; crushing. "Swashing blow." Shak.

SELF-SUFFICIENCY: The quality or state of being self-sufficient.
SCROBICULATE: Having numerous small, shallow depressions or hollows; pitted.
SILICON: A nonmetalic element analogous to carbon. SCARAB: Any one of numerous species of lamellicorn beetles of the genus Scarabæus, or family Scarabæidæ, especially the sacred, or Egyptian, species (Scarabæus sacer, and S. Egyptiorum).

SINUPALLIATE: Having a pallial sinus. See under Sinus.
SARCOLACTIC: relating to muscle and milk; as, sarcolactic acid. See Lactic acid, under Lactic.
SWASHY: Soft, like fruit that is too ripe; quashy; swash. [Prov. Eng.]

SACCHOLACTIC: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid now called mucic acid; saccholic. [Obs.]
SLOCK: To quench; to allay; to slake. See Slake. [Obs. or Scot.]
SUBTREASURER: The public officer who has charge of a subtreasury. [U. S.]
SCARIOSE: Thin, dry, membranous, and not green. Gray.

SUBZYGOMATIC: Situated under the zygoma or zygomatic process.

STRETCHING: from Stretch, v. Stretching course (Masonry), a course or series of stretchers. See Stretcher, 2. Britton.

SUDDENTY: Suddenness; a sudden. [Scot.] On a suddenty, on a sudden. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
SENSATE: To feel or apprehend more or less distinctly through a sense, or the senses; as, to sensate light, or an odor. As those of the one are sensated by the ear, so those of the other are by the eye. R. Hooke. Felt or apprehended through a sense, or the senses. [R.] Baxter.
SMOLDRY: Smoldering; suffocating; smothery. [Obs.] A flaming fire ymixt with smoldry smoke. Spenser.
SPEECHLESS: 1. Destitute or deprived of the faculty of speech. 2. Not speaking for a time; dumb; mute; silent. Speechless with wonder, and half dead with fear. Addison. -- Speech"less*ly, adv. -- Speech"less*ness, n.
STEREO-CHEMIC: Pertaining to, or illustrating, the hypothetical space relations of atoms in the molecule; as, a stereo-chemic formula.
SUBAGENT: A person employed by an agent to transact the whole, or a part, of the business intrusted to the latter. Bouvier. Chitty.
SCHOOLHOUSE: A house appropriated for the use of a school or schools, or for instruction.
SPARSE: 1. Thinly scattered; set or planted here and there; not being dense or close together; as, a sparse population. Carlyle. 2. (Bot.) Placed irregularly and distantly; scattered; -- applied to branches, leaves, peduncles, and the like. To scatter; to disperse. [Obs.] Spenser.
SIDEPIECE: The jamb, or cheek, of an opening in a wall, as of door or window.
SEMINIFIC: Forming or producing seed, or the male generative product of animals or of plants.

SELF-REVERENCE: A reverent respect for one's self. Tennyson.

SHEEPY: Resembling sheep; sheepish. Testament of Love.
SLEETY: Of or pertaining to sleet; characterized by sleet; as, a sleety storm; sleety weather.
SYLLABIFY: To form or divide into syllables.
STEEPEN: To become steep or steeper. As the way steepened . . . I could detect in the hollow of the hill some traces of the old path. H. Miller.
SELF-COMMUNION: Communion with one's self; thoughts about one's self.
SOFTENER: One who, or that which, softens. [Written also, less properly, softner.]
STANCE: 1. A stanza. [Obs.] Chapman. 2. A station; a position; a site. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
SUBQUADRATE: Nearly or approximately square; almost square.

SUPERPRAISE: To praise to excess. To vow, and swear, and superpraise my parts. Shak.
SCOUNDRELDOM: The domain or sphere of scoundrels; scoundrels, collectively; the state, ideas, or practices of scoundrels. Carlyle.
SELF-SEEKING: Seeking one's own interest or happiness; selfish. Arbuthnot. The act or habit of seeking one's own interest or happiness; selfishness.
SEMIQUADRATE: An aspect of the planets when distant from each other the half of a quadrant, or forty-five degrees, or one sign and a half. Hutton.
SOLDIERWOOD: A showy leguminous plant (Calliandra purpurea) of the West Indies. The flowers have long tassels of purple stamens.
SCLEROTAL: Sclerotic. -- n. The optic capsule; the sclerotic coat of the eye. Owen.
STOND: 1. Stop; halt; hindrance. [Obs.] Bacon. 2. A stand; a post; a station. [Obs.] Spenser. To stand. [Obs.] Chaucer.
SIDE-TAKING: A taking sides, as with a party, sect, or faction. Bp. Hall.
SPECIFIABLE: Admitting specification; capable of being specified.
SEMBLING: The practice of attracting the males of Lepidoptera or other insects by exposing the female confined in a cage. Note: It is often adopted by collectors in order to procure specimens of rare species.
STRUTHIONES: (a) A division, or order, of birds, including only the African ostriches. (b) In a wider sense, an extensive group of birds including the ostriches, cassowaries, emus, moas, and allied birds incapable of flight. In this sense it is equivalent to Ratitæ, or Dromæognathæ.

SUBLEVATION: 1. The act of raising on high; elevation. Sir T. More. 2. An uprising; an insurrection. [R.] Sir W. Temple.

SUBPOLYGONAL: Approximately polygonal; somewhat or almost polygonal.

SIGHING: Uttering sighs; grieving; lamenting. "Sighing millions." Cowper. -- Sigh"ing*ly, adv.

SUBWORKER: A subordinate worker or helper. South.
SUBCORACOID: Situated under the coracoid process of the scapula; as, the subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus.
STETHOSCOPICAL: Of or pertaining to a stethoscope; obtained or made by means of a stethoscope. -- Steth`o*scop"ic*al*ly, adv.
SEEKER: 1. One who seeks; that which is used in seeking or searching. 2. (Eccl.) One of a small heterogeneous sect of the 17th century, in Great Britain, who professed to be seeking the true church, ministry, and sacraments. SULTRY: 1. Very hot, burning, and oppressive; as, Libya's sultry deserts. Such as, born beneath the burning sky And sultry sun, betwixt the tropics lie. Dryden. 2. SINGLE-HANDED: Having but one hand, or one workman; also, alone; unassisted.

SEMI-ARIANISM: The doctrines or tenets of the Semi-Arians.
SOLDANRIE: The country ruled by a soldan, or sultan. [Poet.] Sir W. Scott.
SKEG: 1. A sort of wild plum. [Obs.] Holland. 2. pl. A kind of oats. Farm. Encyc. 3. (Naut.) The after part of the keel of a vessel, to which the rudder is attached.
SPLAYMOUTH: A wide mouth; a mouth stretched in derision. Dryden.
SUBCRANIAL: Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the cranium; facial.
SHOPBOARD: A bench or board on which work is performed; a workbench. South.
SHAW: 1. A thicket; a small wood or grove. [Obs. or Prov.Eng. & Scot.] Burns. Gaillard he was as goldfinch in the shaw. Chaucer. The green shaws, the merry green woods. Howitt. 2. pl. The leaves and tops of vegetables, as of potatoes, turnips, etc. [Scot.] Jamieson.
SPONSOR: 1. One who binds himself to answer for another, and is responsible for his default; a surety. 2. One who at the baptism of an infant professore the christian faith in its name, and guarantees its religious education; a godfather or godmother.
SUBHASTATION: A public sale or auction. [R.] Bp. Burnet.
SUINE: A mixture of oleomargarine with lard or other fatty ingredients. It is used as a substitute for butter. See Butterine.
SCIOMACHY: A fighting with a shadow; a mock contest; an imaginary or futile combat. [Written also scimachy.] Cowley.
SPHERULITIC: Of or pertaining to a spherulite; characterized by the presence of spherulites.

SCABLING: A fragment or chip of stone. [Written also scabline.]

SUBDIACONATE: Of or pertaining to a subdeacon, or to the office or rank of a subdeacon. The office or rank of a subdeacon.

SNEAK-CUP: One who sneaks from his cups; one who balks his glass. [Obs.] Shak.

SLUICY: Falling copiously or in streams, as from a sluice. And oft whole sheets descend of sluicy rain. Dryden.

SUBHUMERATE: To place the shoulders under; to bear. [Obs.] Nothing surer ties a friend than freely to subhumerate the burden which was his. Feltham.

SOUND-BOARD: A sounding-board. To many a row of pipes the sound-board breathes. Milton.

SMELLING SALTS: An aromatic preparation of carbonate of ammonia and, often, some scent, to avoid or relieve faintness, headache, or the like.
SKAG: An additional piece fastened to the keel of a boat to prevent lateral motion. See Skeg.
SCHOOLMAN: One versed in the niceties of academical disputation or of school divinity. SHOEING-HORN: 1. A curved piece of polished horn, wood, or metal used to facilitate the entrance of the foot into a shoe. 2. SCRUZE: To squeeze, compress, crush, or bruise. [Obs. or Low] Spenser.

STEREOSCOPICAL: Of or pertaining to the stereoscope; characteristic of, or adapted to, the stereoscope; as, a stereoscopic effect; the stereoscopic function of the eyeglasses; stereoscopic views. -- Ste`re*o*scop"ic*al*ly, adv.

SUPERFAMILY: A group intermediate between a family and a suborder.
SPASTICITY: 1. A state of spasm. 2. The tendency to, or capability of suffering, spasm.
SUPRACRANIAL: Situated above, or in the roof of, the cranium.

SUBSACRAL: Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the sacrum.

SHIFTLESS: Destitute of expedients, or not using successful expedients; characterized by failure, especially by failure to provide for one's own support, through negligence or incapacity; hence, lazy; improvident; thriftless; as, a shiftless fellow; shiftless management. -- Shift"less*ly, adv. -- Shift"less*ness, n.
SIPHONAL: Of or pertaining to a siphon; resembling a siphon. Siphonal stomach (Zoöl.), a stomach which is tubular and bent back upon itself, like a siphon, as in the salmon.
SOLIFIDIAN: One who maintains that faith alone, without works, is sufficient for justification; -- opposed to nullifidian. Hammond. Holding the tenets of Solifidians; of or pertaining to the solifidians.
SCRIMP: To make too small or short; to limit or straiten; to put on short allowance; to scant; to contract; to shorten; as, to scrimp the pattern of a coat. Short; scanty; curtailed. A pinching miser; a niggard. [U.S.]
SUGGEST: 1. To introduce indirectly to the thoughts; to cause to be thought of, usually by the agency of other objects. Some ideas . . . are suggested to the mind by all the ways of sensation and reflection. Locke. 2. To propose with difference or modesty; to hint; to intimate; as, to suggest a difficulty. 3. To seduce; to prompt to evil; to tempt. [Obs....
SWEAL: To melt and run down, as the tallow of a candle; to waste away without feeding the flame. [Written also swale.] Sir W. Scott. To singe; to scorch; to swale; as, to sweal a pig by singeing off the hair.
SUBDIVIDE: To divide the parts of (anything) into more parts; to part into smaller divisions; to divide again, as what has already been divided. The progenies of Cham and Japhet swarmed into colonies, and those colonies were subdivided into many others. Dryden. To be, or to become, subdivided.
SHAME: 1. A painful sensation excited by a consciousness of guilt or impropriety, or of having done something which injures reputation, or of the exposure of that which nature or modesty prompts us to conceal. HIde, for shame, Romans, your grandsires' images, That blush at their degenerate progeny. Dryden. Have you no modesty, no maiden shame Shak. 2. ...
SURFEIT-WATER: Water for the cure of surfeits. [Obs.] Locke.
SABLE: 1. (Zoöl.) A carnivorous animal of the Weasel family (Mustela zibellina) native of the northern latitudes of Europe, Asia, and America, -- noted for its fine, soft, and valuable fur. STEP: 1. To move the foot in walking; to advance or recede by raising and moving one of the feet to another resting place, or by moving both feet in succession. 2. To walk; to go on foot; esp., to walk a little distance; as, to step to one of the neighbors. 3. To walk slowly, gravely, or resolutely. Home the swain retreats, His flock before him steppi...
SPECULATORY: 1. Intended or adapted for viewing or espying; having oversight. T. Warton. 2. Exercising speculation; speculative. T. Carew.
SEA CUCUMBER: Any large holothurian, especially one of those belonging to the genus Pentacta, or Cucumaria, as the common American and European species. (P. frondosa).
SILVERFIN: A small North American fresh-water cyprinoid fish (Notropis Whipplei).
SALLY LUNN: A tea cake slighty sweetened, and raised with yeast, baked in the form of biscuits or in a thin loaf, and eaten hot with butter.
SHOER: One who fits shoes to the feet; one who furnishes or puts on shoes; as, a shoer of horses.
SAGITTARIUS: (a) The ninth of the twelve signs of the zodiac, which the sun enters about November 22, marked thus [&sagittarius;] in almanacs; the Archer. (b) A zodiacal constellation, represented on maps and globes as a centaur shooting an arrow.
SUBARCUATE: Having a figure resembling that of a bow; somewhat curved or arched.
SCIRRHOSITY: A morbid induration, as of a gland; stste of being scirrhous.
SPECTATRIX: A female beholder or looker-on. "A spectatress of the whole scene." Jeffrey.
SHEATHLESS: Without a sheath or case for covering; unsheathed.
SOND: That which is sent; a message or messenger; hence, also, a visitation of providence; an affliction or trial. [Obs.] Ye have enough, parde, of Goddes sond. Chaucer.
SPARROWWORT: An evergreen shrub of the genus Erica (E. passerina).
SQUAMOZYGOMATIC: Of or pertaining to both the squamosal and zygomatic bones; -- applied to a bone, or a center of ossification, in some fetal skulls. -- n. A squamozygomatic bone.
STATIVE: Of or pertaining to a fixed camp, or military posts or quarters. [Obs. or R.]
SEA PURSE: The horny egg case of a skate, and of certain sharks.
SOL: 1. The sun. 2. (Alchem.) Gold; -- so called from its brilliancy, color, and value. Chaucer. (a) A syllable applied in solmization to the note G, or to the fifth tone of any diatonic scale. (b) The tone itself. 1. A sou. 2. A silver and gold coin of Peru. The silver sol is the unit of value, and is worth about 68 cents.
SHUFFLER: 1. One who shuffles. 2. (Zoöl.) Either one of the three common American scaup ducks. See Scaup duck, under Scaup.
SUBSELLIUM: One of the stalls of the lower range where there are two ranges. See Illust. of Stall.
SUBPURCHASER: A purchaser who buys from a purchaser; one who buys at second hand.
SUPRASCALPULARY: Situated above, or on the anterior side of, the scapula.
